title: Why Mistakes Are Your Best English Teachers
focus: Conditionals and linkers of contrast and result
paragraphs: When I was fifteen, I was terrified of speaking English in class. I knew the grammar well, but I stayed silent because I thought that a mistake would make me look stupid. My teacher, Mr Brown, noticed this and told me something that I still remember: 'If you never make mistakes, you are not trying hard enough.'

That weekend, I decided to test his idea. I went to a bookshop in the city centre and asked in English for a book. Unfortunately, I said, 'I want to buy a book in the library.' The seller smiled and kindly explained that a library lends books, but a bookshop sells them. I was as red as a tomato, but I never forgot the difference again.

This is the main reason why mistakes help us. When we make them in real situations, our brain connects the correction with an emotion and a memory. It is much easier to remember the day you said 'library' in a bookshop than a word from a list. Many teachers also believe that students who speak more, even with errors, improve faster than students who only write.

Of course, mistakes are not useful if we ignore them. Here are three simple habits that have worked for me. First, I keep a small notebook where I write my errors and the correct versions. Second, I ask friends to correct me, and I thank them every time. Third, I record myself for one minute every week and listen carefully for patterns.

Fear is natural, but it shouldn't control you. If you wait until your English is perfect, you will never start. Instead, accept that mistakes are part of the journey. Today I study at university, and I speak English every day with classmates from different countries. I still make mistakes, but now I smile when I notice them, and I think of Mr Brown.

title: Three Days Behind the Stage
paragraphs: When my friend Nuria told me that the River Sounds Festival needed volunteers, I said yes immediately. I imagined myself dancing in front of the stage while my favourite bands played. The reality was different, but also much more interesting.

Our team had twenty volunteers, and our first job on Friday was to prepare thousands of wristbands. We arrived at seven in the morning, got a yellow T-shirt and a radio, and listened to a long safety talk. The coordinator, a calm woman named Mrs Anand, repeated one sentence all day: 'Check twice, and always smile.'

I worked at the information tent. People asked me about everything: where the toilets were, what time their favourite band was playing and how to find a lost phone. By Saturday afternoon I knew the map of the festival so well that I could answer without looking. My feet hurt, but I felt useful and proud.

The most dramatic moment happened on Saturday evening. A little boy of about five came to the tent alone, crying, and could only say his name and 'blue shoes'. We announced his description on the radio, and in less than ten minutes a very worried father ran towards us. He hugged his son and then hugged me too. I almost cried myself.

In total, I worked about thirty hours over three days, and I didn't see more than four songs. In exchange, I got free entry on Sunday, two meals a day and a group of new friends. If you are thinking about volunteering, be ready to work hard, wear comfortable shoes and bring a bottle of water. And don't expect to hear every concert: expect to remember the festival for different reasons.

title: The Teenage Voice of Radio Selva
focus: Present perfect, passive voice and relative clauses
paragraphs: In a small village in the Ecuadorian Amazon, where the nearest town is three hours away by canoe and road, the most popular person is a sixteen-year-old radio presenter called Ana Shiguango. Every afternoon at five, her voice is heard in more than twenty villages.

Radio Selva was created ten years ago by the community with the help of a small foundation. Its equipment is simple: a computer, two microphones and an antenna on top of a tall tree. The programmes are broadcast in Kichwa and in Spanish, so that grandparents and children can understand each other.

Ana joined the team two years ago. She began by reading the weather report, and now she presents a programme about teenagers' lives. 'People think that radio is old-fashioned,' she says, 'but here it is the fastest way to tell the news. When the river is rising, we warn the villages in minutes.'

The most popular section is called 'Messages'. Families in remote places send short messages: a mother tells her son that dinner is ready, a farmer announces that he has fresh fruit to sell, and a teacher reminds parents about a meeting. 'It's like a social network without internet,' laughs Ana. 'Everybody listens, and everybody is a little famous.'

The station survives thanks to donations. Last year, listeners gave about eight hundred dollars to buy a new microphone, and a university in Quito sent two volunteers to teach editing to the teenagers. Ana wants to study journalism, but she isn't planning to leave her village. 'I want to get a degree, and then come back,' she says. 'This is my community, and it needs voices that love it.'

title: Gap Year: Yes or No?
paragraphs: After finishing secondary school, some young people take a 'gap year': a year without studying, to travel, work or volunteer before starting university. Is it a great idea or a waste of time? Two students give their opinions.

Isabela, 18, says yes. 'If I went to university now, I would be exhausted before the first class. I have studied hard for twelve years, and I don't really know what I want to do. If I spent a year working in a hostel in another country, I would improve my English and discover my interests. I think students who take a gap year choose their courses more carefully.'

Tariq, 18, disagrees. 'I understand that idea, but I think there is a big risk. If I stopped studying for a year, I might lose my habit of working hard, and it could be difficult to start again. My cousin took a gap year, and in the end he never went to university. Also, a year of travelling is expensive, and not every family can pay for it.'

Isabela answers that a gap year doesn't have to be expensive. 'You could work in your own city, learn a skill or volunteer in a local organisation. If you saved money for six months, you could also travel for six months. The most important thing is to have a plan.'

Tariq accepts that a plan is essential, but he suggests another option: 'I would study and work at the same time, or take a short break during the summer. In that way, I wouldn't lose time, and I would still have new experiences.' Both agree on one point: you should talk to your family, to your teachers and to people who have already made the decision before choosing.

title: The Girl Who Builds Robots from Scrap
focus: Present perfect, past simple and relative clauses
paragraphs: In a small workshop behind her family's house in Nairobi, seventeen-year-old Wanjiru Kamau is building a robot that can carry a glass of water without spilling it. The robot's arms are made from the tubes of an old vacuum cleaner, and its eyes are two broken phone cameras. Everything comes from objects that other people threw away.

Her interest in engineering began when she was nine. 'My uncle gave me a broken radio, and I opened it just to see what was inside,' she remembers. 'I was surprised that something so complicated could be made of small, simple parts. After that, I started to take apart every machine I could find.'

Finding the parts is not always easy. Every Saturday, Wanjiru visits the markets where people sell used electronics, and she has learnt to recognise good components. She also uses the internet to learn: she has watched hundreds of free videos and has taught herself basic programming. 'I didn't wait for a perfect laboratory. I started with what I had,' she says.

Last year she began teaching a small group of eleven-year-olds in her neighbourhood. Every Sunday afternoon, the children come to her workshop and build simple machines with batteries, wires and cardboard. 'The first rule is that mistakes are welcome,' Wanjiru tells them. 'If your machine doesn't work, you have discovered one way that doesn't work.'

Her dream is to study mechanical engineering at a university and design cheap medical equipment for rural clinics. 'There are many problems that could be solved with simple, affordable machines,' she says. 'But solutions are often invented by people who are close to the problem.' Meanwhile, her water-carrying robot will take part in a school science fair next month, and Wanjiru hopes that it will not spill a single drop.

title: The Last Bus Home
paragraphs: Noemí was walking quickly along a quiet street in Quito when she realised that she had made a mistake. The orchestra rehearsal at her school had finished at nine, but she had stayed to help her friends put away the instruments. Now it was ten o'clock, and the last bus had already left.

Her phone had no battery, so she couldn't call her parents. She stood under a street light and tried to think. The nearest main road was about twenty minutes away on foot. She wasn't afraid of the dark, but the street was very empty, and the only sound was a dog barking in the distance.

Then she saw a small light at the end of the street. It belonged to a security booth, where an old man in a grey uniform was drinking tea and listening to the radio. 'Good evening,' Noemí said, trying to sound calm. 'I'm sorry to bother you. Could I use your phone, please? I missed my bus.'

The man, whose name was Don Aurelio, looked at her carefully and then smiled. 'Of course, young lady,' he said. He gave her his phone and a chair, and he even offered her a cup of hot tea. While she was calling her mother, Don Aurelio went to the corner and stopped a taxi. 'I know this driver,' he told her. 'He lives near my house, and he is very responsible.'

Twenty minutes later, Noemí was at home. Her mother, who had been waiting at the door with a worried face, hugged her for a long time. 'Next time, tell me before you stay late,' she said. Noemí promised, and she also decided to carry a small battery charger in her bag. The next afternoon, she took a thank-you card and a box of biscuits to the security booth.

title: Six Months in Sydney: What I Miss and What I Love
paragraphs: Six months ago I left Bogotá to study English and work in Sydney. People asked me if I was scared, and the honest answer is yes. Now I want to share what I have learnt, what I miss and what has surprised me.

What I miss is simple: my family, my friends and, strangely, the food. In Sydney there are excellent restaurants, but I haven't found a decent arepa yet. Last month I tried to make one myself, and my flatmates, who had never eaten one, loved it. So I think I am becoming an unofficial ambassador for Colombian food.

What surprised me most is the language. I studied English for years, but nobody told me that Australians shorten almost every word. 'Afternoon' becomes 'arvo', and 'breakfast' becomes 'brekkie'. At the beginning I understood nothing in my part-time job at a café. Now I use these words myself, and my accent is a mixture that makes everybody laugh.

Some things are the same everywhere. People are kind when you are lost, and a smile helps in every language. However, the calendar was confusing at first. Christmas was in the middle of summer, and my colleagues celebrated with a barbecue on the beach. It was great, but I felt strange wearing shorts and sunglasses while listening to Christmas songs.

I haven't decided yet if I will stay another year. On the one hand, I have made good friends and my English has improved a lot. On the other hand, I am far from home, and sometimes the distance feels very heavy. For now, I call my mum every Sunday, and I keep a photo of my street on the wall. If you are thinking about studying abroad, my advice is: do it, but prepare your heart as well as your suitcase.
glossary: de medio tiempo, de jornada parcial

title: The Chess Club Nobody Joined
focus: Past simple, past perfect and time clauses
paragraphs: When Mr Ortega, the maths teacher, announced a chess club at the beginning of the school year at a school in Bogotá, he was sure that at least twenty students would join. On the first Thursday, he waited in room 12 with eight chessboards. Only one student came: Ibrahim, a quiet boy from Year 8, who sat down and said, 'Hello, sir. Do you want to play?'

For a month, the club was just the two of them. They played, they talked about openings and Mr Ortega told stories about famous matches. Some teachers laughed in the corridor and called it 'the smallest club in the school'. Mr Ortega started to wonder if he should cancel it, but Ibrahim never missed a Thursday.

One day Ibrahim had an idea. 'Why don't we play outside during break?' he asked. The next morning, they carried a chessboard to the yard and set it on a bench. At first, people only looked. Then a girl asked what the pieces were called, and a boy wanted to try. By the end of the week, six students were queueing to play.

Soon the club became popular. Students liked that it was relaxed: you could arrive late, play one game and leave. Mr Ortega moved the meeting to a bigger room, and Ibrahim, who used to be shy, began to teach beginners how to move the pieces. 'The knight is the strangest one,' he explained. 'It jumps, and that's why it surprises people.'

Last month, the school organised its first chess tournament, with thirty-two players. Ibrahim reached the semi-final and lost, but he wasn't upset. 'I won something more important,' he said. 'I have a club full of friends.' Mr Ortega, who had almost given up in October, felt very proud. On Monday he hung a sign on the door: 'Chess Club: now with room for everyone.'

title: How Do Weather Forecasts Work?
paragraphs: Will it rain tomorrow? Millions of people ask this question every morning, and weather forecasts try to answer it. But how do experts know what will happen in the sky? The answer is a mix of observation, mathematics and powerful computers.

First, the experts collect data. Thousands of weather stations around the world measure temperature, wind, humidity and pressure. Satellites take pictures of clouds from space, and radars show where it is raining. Many weather services also release balloons that carry instruments high into the atmosphere. All this information arrives every few hours.

Second, a supercomputer uses all this information to create a model of the atmosphere. The model divides the planet into millions of small boxes and calculates how the air in each box will change in the next hours and days. These calculations are so complex that they would take a person many years to do by hand.

However, forecasts are not perfect. The atmosphere is a chaotic system, which means that a tiny change today can cause a big difference next week. For this reason, forecasts for the next three days are usually reliable, but forecasts for ten days away are much less accurate. Experts often run the model many times with small changes to see how the results vary.

That is also why forecasters talk about probabilities. A 'seventy per cent chance of rain' usually means that in similar conditions it rained in seven out of ten cases. It doesn't mean that it will rain for seventy per cent of the day. Next time you check your weather app, remember how much work is behind it, and take an umbrella if the chance is high. Better safe than sorry!

title: New Year's Resolutions That Actually Work
focus: Will vs going to, advice and instructions
paragraphs: At midnight on 31 December, millions of people around the world make promises to themselves. In Spain, many people eat twelve grapes, one for each chime of the clock, and in several Latin American countries some families walk around the block with a suitcase to attract a year full of travel. Whatever the tradition, the idea is the same: next year will be better.

The problem is that many resolutions are forgotten by February. Why does this happen? Often our goals are too big or too vague. 'I'm going to be healthier' sounds great, but it doesn't say what to do on Monday morning. When the first week of enthusiasm ends, we don't know how to continue.

Experts suggest starting with small, specific actions. Instead of 'I will learn English', try 'I will study twenty minutes every day after dinner.' Instead of 'I'll save money', try 'I'll put five euros in a box every Friday.' A small goal is easier to measure, and every time you complete it, you feel a little success that motivates you to continue.

Another useful idea is to tell somebody. If a friend knows about your plan, you will feel more responsible. Better still, find a friend with a similar goal, and check in with each other every week. You can also keep a calendar on the wall and mark each successful day with a cross. After two weeks, the chain of crosses becomes something you don't want to break.

Finally, be kind to yourself. Everyone has bad days, and missing one session doesn't mean failure. If you forget your goal on Tuesday, simply restart on Wednesday. Real change is not a straight line. It looks more like a path with hills and curves. So this year, make fewer promises, choose one that matters to you, and give it a real chance.

questions.q: In Spain, many people eat twelve grapes at midnight on New Year's Eve.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice: 'In Spain, many people eat twelve grapes, one for each chime of the clock'.

questions.q: Experts say that resolutions should be as big as possible.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice que muchas metas fracasan por ser demasiado grandes o vagas y recomienda 'small, specific actions'.

questions.q: Why are many resolutions forgotten by February?
options: The goals are too big or too vague
People only make them because of tradition
People have no free time
questions.explain_es: El texto dice: 'Often our goals are too big or too vague'.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest to feel more responsible?
options: Tell a friend about your plan
Write a long diary every night
Buy a special notebook for goals
questions.explain_es: El texto dice: 'Another useful idea is to tell somebody. If a friend knows about your plan, you will feel more responsible'.

questions.q: What does 'Real change is not a straight line' suggest?
options: Change is impossible for most people
Change is always fast and easy
Progress includes difficult moments
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: lo compara con 'a path with hills and curves'; el progreso incluye altibajos, y por eso hay que ser amable consigo mismo.

questions.q: Mark each successful day with a ____ on the calendar.
questions.explain_es: El texto dice: 'mark each successful day with a cross'.

questions.q: In 'walk around the block', 'block' means…
options: a shop that sells travel bags
a heavy piece of stone
a group of buildings between streets
questions.explain_es: 'Block' = cuadra o manzana, el grupo de edificios entre cuatro calles.
